DOCUMENT R01 — System frequency record, 9 August 2019, 16:40-17:45 BST
Owner/originator: National Grid ESO (NESO published dataset)
Record type: measured time-series extract (CSV file) with this metadata note
STATUS: REAL MEASURED DATA EXTRACT — frequency values are unchanged from the published dataset;
only a time slice was selected and the columns were renamed and reformatted as described below.
Clock reference: every timestamp in the CSV carries an explicit +01:00 offset (BST = UTC+01:00).
Value-status legend: [measured] = value from the published measurement dataset. Every frequency value
in the CSV is [measured]. This note adds no measured values of its own beyond the sample rows quoted.

SOURCE DATASET
Publisher: NESO data portal (api.neso.energy), monthly system frequency archive for August 2019.
Archive file: f-2019-8.zip; member file "f 2019 8.csv"; columns "dtm" (date-time) and "f" (Hz).
Published date-time format: "2019-08-09 16:40:00 +0100" (local time with an explicit +0100 offset).
Publisher's correction note: the publisher's historical data page states that 2019 data was corrected
on 14 February 2020. This extract comes from the archive as downloaded for this exercise (member file
dated 14 February 2020); it is not a preserved copy of the data as originally published in 2019.

EXTRACT
Slice: 2019-08-09T16:40:00+01:00 (inclusive) to 2019-08-09T17:45:00+01:00 (exclusive).
First sample: 2019-08-09T16:40:00+01:00. Last sample: 2019-08-09T17:44:59+01:00.
Rows: 3900 data rows after one header row.
Interval: 1 second between consecutive rows. Checked at extraction: no missing seconds, no duplicate
timestamps, timestamps strictly increasing.
Unit: hertz (Hz).
Values: copied from column "f" without rounding, smoothing, resampling or interpolation.
Number format: decimals are written without trailing zeros, so the number of decimal places varies
(at most 3); for example a published value of 50 appears as 50.0.
Resolution: one published value per second. The file carries no information about behaviour between
consecutive samples and no description of the measurement method.

TIME BASIS
The published +0100 offsets were parsed as supplied (offset-aware), not treated as naive UTC, and are
written in ISO-8601 form as +01:00. UTC = BST minus one hour, e.g. 2019-08-09T16:40:00+01:00 is
2019-08-09T15:40:00Z. The publisher's general dataset description refers to UTC while the raw file
carries +0100 offsets; no further publisher clarification was obtained. The offsets were used as given.

FILE AND COLUMNS
Artifact: frequency_2019-08-09_1640-1745_BST.csv, delivered with this document. After retrieval it is
in this document's evidence folder: $EVIDENCE_DIR/R01/frequency_2019-08-09_1640-1745_BST.csv

Column timestamp: ISO-8601 date-time with explicit offset, e.g. 2019-08-09T16:40:00+01:00.
Column frequency_hz: system frequency in Hz (decimal number).

Time: time:<ISO-8601> or time:<start>/<end>, each with an explicit offset (Z or +01:00) and within

DOCUMENT R03 — Transmission fault and protection records, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: National Grid Electricity Transmission (NGET); lightning detection data: MeteoGroup
Record type: compiled circuit fault, protection, auto-reclose, power quality and lightning records
STATUS: RECONSTRUCTED FOR EVALUATION FROM PUBLISHED RECORDS — NOT AN ORIGINAL SYSTEM EXPORT.
Entries are compiled from published post-event investigation reports; layout and wording are reconstructions.
Sections A-F are records; section G holds later, attributed assessments.
Clock reference: BST (UTC+01:00). The sources do not label the clock of the B3 and section C times; they are
read as BST because the ESO report dates this event at 4:52pm, and are written with +01:00. Times with no
such anchor (B2, section E) are marked "clock basis not stated" and are written without an offset.
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated by the record owner in published material;
[estimated] value the record owner describes as an estimate; [measured] and [illustrative] not used.

SECTION A — CIRCUIT AND NETWORK CONTEXT
A1  Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main: 400 kV [reported] double-circuit overhead line of just over 35 km [reported],
    from Eaton Socon substation (near St Neots, Cambridgeshire) to Wymondley Main substation (near Stevenage,
    Hertfordshire). Lattice steel towers carry two circuits, each with 3 [reported] conductors (phases) on one
    side of the tower, and an earth wire at the top of the tower.
A2  Planned outage on 9 August 2019: the Killingholme–Keadby circuit was out of service for planned
    maintenance; the NGET power quality monitor connected to it, close to Killingholme, was unavailable.

SECTION B — LIGHTNING DETECTION RECORDS (MeteoGroup data, as reported by ESO and NGET)
B1  9 August 2019, 24 hours [reported]: 12,370 [reported] lightning strikes across mainland UK.
B2  2 hours [reported] preceding 17:00 [reported] (clock basis not stated): 2,106 [reported] strikes across
    mainland UK.
B3  2019-08-09T16:52:33+01:00 [reported]: three [reported] almost simultaneous lightning strikes recorded
    adjacent to the Eaton Socon–Wymondley circuit, close to Willian Arboretum, at the Wymondley end of the
    circuit.
B4  Location uncertainty: each strike is plotted with a radius of uncertainty for the location of the direct
    hit; any of the three strikes could have hit the circuit.
B5  Largest of the three strikes: current amplitude 33.7 kA [reported].
B6  NGET overlay of MeteoGroup activity near the circuit: a number of strikes close to NGET overhead line
    circuits; one strike is timed at the same time as the fault; the activity aligns with protection data
    indicating the fault was 4.5 km [reported] from Wymondley Main, just outside Letchworth Garden City.

SECTION C — FAULT AND PROTECTION RECORD, EATON SOCON–WYMONDLEY MAIN CIRCUIT (times read as BST, +01:00)
C1  2019-08-09T16:52:33.490+01:00 [reported]: fault inception. Single (blue) phase to earth fault on one Eaton
    Socon–Wymondley circuit: the middle conductor (blue phase) faulted to the earthed tower.
C2  Fault location: approximately 4.5 km [reported] along the circuit from the Wymondley Main end.
C3  Fault infeed: approximately 21 kA (RMS) [reported] from Wymondley Main; approximately
    7 kA (RMS) [reported] from Eaton Socon.
C4  Blue-phase voltage during the fault: estimated 50% [estimated] depression (ESO timeline); NGET: circa
    50% [reported] at the fault location, lasting 100 ms [reported] in the vicinity of the fault.
C5  2019-08-09T16:52:33.560+01:00 [reported]: Wymondley Main end opens to clear the fault; main protection
    operating time 70 ms [reported] after fault inception.
C6  2019-08-09T16:52:33.564+01:00 [reported]: Eaton Socon end opens to clear the fault; main protection
    operating time 74 ms [reported] after fault inception.
C7  Requirement cited by NGET, Grid Code Connection Condition CC.6.2.3.1.1, primary protection fault clearance
    times: 80 ms at 400 kV [reported]; 100 ms at 275 kV [reported]; 120 ms at 132 kV and below [reported].
C8  2019-08-09T16:52:53+01:00 [reported]: Eaton Socon–Wymondley circuit energised on Delayed Auto-Reclose
    (DAR), returning it to service about 20 seconds [reported] after the fault.
C9  DAR was available and in service on the circuit. After the reclose the network was in the same
    configuration as before the event; no further operational intervention or immediate site attendance was
    required.

SECTION D — POWER QUALITY AND VOLTAGE RECORDS (measured magnitudes as published; assessments are in G)
D1  Ryhall 400 kV [reported] (the next substation along from Eaton Socon): blue-phase voltage depression
    44% [reported]; duration of the event including voltage recovery 100 ms [reported].
D2  Ryhall: a further small transient after the fault; NGET text: a minute [reported] after the fault;
    figure annotation: 2 mins [reported] after the fault. It did not register at Necton.
D3  Necton 400 kV [reported] (Norfolk; electrically further from the fault): blue-phase voltage depression
    21% [reported]; duration including voltage recovery 80 ms [reported].
D4  ESO system measurements: voltages recovered to normal less than 100 ms [reported] after the circuit was
    de-energised; the dip was larger at locations near the short circuit, the largest at Wymondley.
D5  Area of the event: harmonics less than 1% [reported]; negative phase sequence (NPS) currents did not
    exceed 0.6% [reported].

SECTION E — OTHER CIRCUIT TRIPS ON 9 AUGUST 2019 (times as printed; clock basis not stated in the sources)
E1  Harker–Stella West 275 kV [reported] circuit. ESO report narrative: at 14:23 [reported] the circuit was
    tripped and automatically returned to service; lightning was observed active in the vicinity; there
    were no adverse effects to the transmission system following this fault. ESO answers to E3C questions
    (Appendix M, Q30): tripped at 14:23:00 [reported]; returned to service via Delayed Auto Reclose (DAR)
    at 14:23:32 [reported].
E2  Blyth–Eccles–Stella West 400 kV [reported] circuit. ESO report narrative: at 16:50:44 [reported] lightning
    struck the circuit near Longframlington, Northumberland; the circuit tripped and closed with no power
    losses associated. ESO answers to E3C questions (Appendix M, Q30), for the Blyth–Eccles–Stella West 1
    400 kV [reported] circuit: tripped at 16:43:25 [reported]; returned to service via DAR at
    16:43:54 [reported]; lightning observed in the vicinity; fault cleared with no adverse effects.

SECTION F — SITE FOLLOW-UP (NGET)
F1  After the event: engineers attended Wymondley Main and Eaton Socon substations to collect data, including
    protection operating data; all assets were operating as normal; no defects identified.
F2  Saturday 10 August 2019, morning: visual inspection of the Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main overhead line; no
    defects observed.

SECTION G — POST-EVENT ASSESSMENTS (attributed later statements; not system records)
G1  NGET report (Appendix C to the ESO technical report of 6 September 2019): the network "operated as
    designed and in line with standards"; main protection cleared the fault within the 80 ms [reported]
    required in the Grid Code; the DAR system operated as expected and designed.
G2  NGET: one of the strikes is timed at the same time as the fault; "As such we can be confident that a
    lightning strike was the cause of the fault."
G3  NGET (power quality analysis and findings): the voltage depressions and durations were as expected for
    this type of fault; electrically further from the fault, voltage dips of 20% [reported] with
    80 ms [reported] duration were observed; the later small transient at Ryhall was most likely associated
    with reactive compensation switching in response to the fault, and was too small to register at Necton.
G4  NGET (steady state, harmonics and NPS): pre-fault and post-fault steady state voltages at Wymondley
    Main, Eaton Socon, Keadby and Killingholme 400 kV [reported] were within the SQSS operational limits of
    ±10% (420 kV to 380 kV) [reported]; harmonics were within the 3% [reported] limit of ER G5/4; NPS
    currents were within the 1.5% [reported] Grid Code limit.
G5  ESO technical report (6 September 2019): all measurements indicate that voltages stayed above the Fault
    Ride Through profile specified in the Grid Code and returned to within steady state limits after the
    event.
G6  ESO technical report: NGET, by analysing its protection data, confirmed that these lightning strikes
    were the cause of the circuit trip and reclose; the transmission system protection operated in line
    with the design and in compliance with the Grid Code requirements on fault clearance.
G7  Ofgem report (3 January 2020): NGET's evidence shows fault clearance times for the two circuit breakers
    under 75 ms [reported] and voltage within a range of 390 kV to 410 kV [reported] following the fault; the
    evidence suggests NGET's transmission assets performed as expected.

DOCUMENT S01 — Hornsea One offshore wind farm event log, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: Ørsted (Hornsea One operator)
Record type: plant configuration note, event log extract and separately dated post-event annotations
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: this reconstructed log is rendered in UTC with an explicit Z suffix. The operator's
published timeline uses local time (16:52:33:490, 16:52:33:728) except one passage, written 15.52.
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated in the operator's published material or in published
accounts of it; [estimated] approximate value derived from a reported description; [measured] and
[illustrative] not used. "~" marks a value the source gives as approximate.

PART 1 — PLANT CONFIGURATION ON 9 AUGUST 2019
P1  Hornsea One: offshore wind farm 120 km [reported] from the Yorkshire coast, under construction offshore;
    1.2 GW [reported] installed capacity when complete (174 [reported] turbines rated 7 MW [reported]).
P2  Three phases of 400 MW [reported] each: Hornsea 1A, Hornsea 1B and Hornsea 1C. Each phase connects to its
    own HVAC collector substation, then an offshore HVAC reactive compensation station, an onshore HVAC
    substation and the National Grid 400 kV [reported] substation at Killingholme.
P3  Two modules fully installed and the third partially installed: declared export capability
    800 MW [reported].
P4  Internal network outage configuration: one SGT and one offshore transmission system user asset (OTSUA)
    circuit on outage.
P5  Hornsea 1B (circuit Z12) operating at 400 MW [reported] before the event (maximum for that unit).

PART 2 — EVENT LOG (raw entries; times UTC, explicit Z)
Time (UTC) and status           Entry
~15:42Z [estimated]             Reactive power output response to a 2% [reported] voltage step change. See
                                note (a) and annotation A5.
15:52:33.000Z-.490Z [reported]  Voltage at the 400 kV [reported] substation steady at ~400 kV [reported].
15:52:33.490Z [estimated]       Unbalanced voltage dip at the Transmission Interface Point (TIP); note (b).
15:52:33.490Z-.700Z [reported]  Reactive compensation control initially injects reactive power (leading MVAr)
                                to boost NETS voltage, then a significant oscillation: absorption
                                >300 MVAr [reported] while NETS and Hornsea One system voltage falls to
                                ~394 kV [reported]; then injection again.
15:52:33.490Z-.700Z [reported]  Active power reduces from 799 MW [reported] to 400 MW [reported], then returns
                                to 799 MW [reported].
15:52:33.531Z [reported]        Status: generating 799 MW [reported]; absorbing 0.4 MVAr [reported].
15:52:33.700Z [reported]        Reactive power passes ~0 MVAr [reported] as it switches rapidly from injection
                                to absorption; Hornsea now absorbs ~560 MVAr [reported].
15:52:33.700Z-.835Z [estimated] In the 34 kV [reported] collection cable system the voltage rapidly reduces
                                to 20 kV [reported] (target voltage 34 kV [reported]); note (c).
15:52:33.728Z [reported]        Hornsea 1B and Hornsea 1C begin de-loading turbines.
15:52:33.835Z [reported]        De-load complete, 107 ms [reported] after it began: all WTGs on Hornsea 1B and
                                1C at 0 MW [reported]. Hornsea 1A remains in operation at 62 MW [reported].
                                Site: stabilised at 62 MW [reported], injecting 21 MVAr [reported].

Compiler's notes on Part 2 (added for this reconstruction; not log content)
(a) ~15:42Z [estimated]: the operator gives no exact time, only 10 minutes [reported] before the event.
(b) The operator times the TIP voltage dip only to the minute; the log uses .490Z, where the
    steady-voltage interval above ends.
(c) The operator gives no separate time for the 20 kV [reported] voltage: it follows the .700Z switch to
    absorption and is described with the de-load that ends at .835Z.

PART 3 — POST-EVENT ANNOTATIONS (added after the event; not contemporaneous log content)
Annotation A — operator investigation report, "Ørsted Technical Report for National Grid ESO on the
events of 9 August 2019", dated 5 September 2019:
A1  Section "Conclusion": "The de-load was caused by an unexpected wind farm control system response, due
    to an insufficiently damped electrical resonance in the sub-synchronous frequency range, which was
    triggered by the initial event."
A2  Initially the wind farm responded as expected by injecting reactive power; in the following few hundred
    milliseconds, as active power reduced and the reactive power balance changed, the majority of the turbines
    were disconnected by automatic protection systems.
A3  Hornsea 1B system voltage falls to ~20 kV [reported] while attempting to maintain full active power,
    which leads to an overcurrent of each WTG on 1B and 1C; the WTGs de-load as part of the industry
    standard protection system to avoid permanent damage to the generators.
A4  Hornsea One's systems identified a weak grid and then detected an unusual voltage disturbance, later found
    to have been caused by a circuit trip on the external 400 kV [reported] network, itself caused by a
    lightning strike. The operator states it is unaware of the exact time of the lightning strike.
A5  Identified after the event, as part of this investigation: electrical oscillations occurring before the
    event, without causing any de-loading. About 10 minutes [reported] before the event (log entry
    ~15:42Z [estimated]; exact time not published), the reactive power response to a 2% [reported] voltage
    step change was a damped oscillatory response from the overall voltage control systems.
A6  Before the event each stage had been modelled and physically tested in line with grid code requirements;
    the potential for oscillations had been considered. To the operator's knowledge this is the first time
    such oscillations have led to a de-load of a wind farm.
A7  A control system software update performed on 10 August 2019 [reported], previously agreed with the
    manufacturer, is stated to mitigate the observed behaviour.
Annotation B — operator statements as reported in the ESO technical report dated 6 September 2019:
B1  Initially the operator understood the Dynamic Reactive Compensator (DRC) to be responsible for the rapid
    de-load; it has since concluded that the DRC worked as designed and was not the cause.
B2  The configuration with one SGT and one OTSUA circuit on outage was a contributory factor as it created a
    weak internal network environment; the operator has since reviewed and reconfigured it.
B3  The wind turbine settings were standard settings from the manufacturer; the turbine controllers reacted
    incorrectly due to an insufficiently damped electrical resonance in the sub-synchronous frequency range,
    so that the local voltage dropped and the turbines shut themselves down.
Annotation C — regulator findings, Ofgem report dated 3 January 2020:
C1  The onshore control system operated as expected when the system voltage dipped; the offshore wind turbine
    controllers reacted incorrectly to voltage fluctuations on the offshore network following the fault,
    causing an instability that triggered two modules to automatically shut down.
C2  The stability issue had occurred around ten minutes [reported] before the incident without causing
    de-loading at that time.
C3  Modelling with the equipment manufacturer before 9 August suggested voltage control performance issues at
    the full planned 1,200 MW [reported]; these were not discussed with the ESO. The software update had been
    planned for 13 August [reported] and was implemented on 10 August [reported].
data.title: Hornsea One offshore wind farm event log, 9 August 2019

DOCUMENT R02 — System conditions data, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: Elexon Limited (BMRS / Insights API data, much of it supplied by the system
operator); National Energy System Operator (NESO) open data portal; National Grid ESO (technical
report tables)
Record type: real public dataset extracts (CSV files) with two published report tables and this
metadata note
STATUS: REAL DATA EXTRACTS WITH TRANSCRIBED REPORT TABLES — dataset values are unchanged from the
publishers' files (only rows and columns were selected); report tables, captions and quotations
are reproduced as printed. Nothing in this record is synthesised.
Clock reference: stated for each file and table below. Elexon timestamps are UTC (ISO-8601 with
Z). Elexon and NESO settlement periods are numbered on the UK local clock: period 1 starts at
00:00 local time and each period lasts 30 minutes. UK local time on 9 August 2019 was BST
(UTC+01:00).
Value-status legend: [measured] metered or observed value as published; [reported] value stated by
its publisher or by a report; [estimated] value its source describes as an estimate; [modelled]
value produced by a model; [digitised] and [illustrative] are not used.

PART A — HOW TO USE THIS RECORD
A1  The CSV files described in Part B are delivered with this note; after retrieval they are in
    $EVIDENCE_DIR/R02/. Dataset values are copied without rounding, unit conversion, interpolation
    or gap filling. CSV conventions for files built from the publishers' JSON: comma-separated,
    UTF-8, LF line endings, one header row; numbers as published; true/false for JSON booleans; an

DOCUMENT S03 — Little Barford power station alarm and sequence-of-events records, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: RWE Generation (Little Barford power station)
Record type: station sequence-of-events (SOE) extract, unit output record and attributed annotations
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: SOE entries are offsets from a datum T recorded by the station's Sequence of Events
system. The operator gives T = 16:52:34 +/- 0.5 s [reported] without stating a clock basis; it is read
here as BST (UTC+01:00). The operator states that further work is needed to align T with the datum
used by the system operator (ESO).
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated in the operator's or the system operator's published
material; [measured], [estimated] and [illustrative] not used.

PART 1 — STATION
S1  Little Barford: 740 MW [reported] combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) station in Bedfordshire,
    connected to the transmission system at the Eaton Socon 400 kV [reported] substation.
S2  Units: two gas turbines (GT1A, GT1B) and one steam turbine (ST1C); all three were operating on
    9 August 2019.

PART 2 — SEQUENCE OF EVENTS (station SOE system; offsets from datum T)
Seq  Event                                     Offset from T
E1   110 V AC UPS -B- general fault alarm      T = 0 ms [reported]
E2   110 V AC UPS -A- general fault alarm      +3 ms [reported]
E3   Initiation of ST control system shutdown  +253 ms [reported]
E4   ST generator breaker open command         +1.16 s [reported]
E5   ST generator breaker open feedback        +1.185 s [reported]
E6   GT1A auto shutdown command                +56.583 s [reported]
E7   GT1A breaker open feedback                +57.620 s [reported]
E8   GT1B manual shutdown command              +83.897 s [reported]
E9   GT1B breaker open feedback                +84.613 s [reported]
SOE note (operator): times are recorded in the station's Sequence of Events system; the operator has
confidence in the chronology of the events.

PART 3 — UNIT OUTPUT AT TRIP (as published by the system operator, ESO technical report)
U1  ST1C steam turbine: 244 MW [reported]
U2  GT1A gas turbine: 210 MW [reported]
U3  GT1B gas turbine: 187 MW [reported]
U4  Total loss at the station: 641 MW [reported]

PART 4 — POST-EVENT ANNOTATIONS (attributed; added after the event, not SOE content)
Annotation A — operator report "RWE Preliminary Findings Regarding the Event on 9th August 2019",
dated 30 August 2019:
A1  Steam turbine: "Our investigations have confirmed that the Steam Turbine tripped due to a
    discrepancy in the speed signals after the point of the Transmission System fault clearance."
A2  Steam turbine: a comprehensive investigation of hardware, software, fault handling and diagnostic
    coverage for the conditions the ST was subjected to during this rare system disturbance is ongoing;
    additional high-resolution frequency data relevant to Eaton Socon has been received from NGESO.
A3  Gas turbines: upon initiation of the steam turbine trip the gas turbines went into bypass mode of
    operation, which is the normal response to allow sustained operation.
A4  GT1A: "For reasons presently unknown a high-pressure excursion occurred on GT1A resulting in an
    automated trip." The operator adds that given the prevailing conditions all systems functioned as
    expected.
A5  GT1B: "GT1B was manually tripped shortly after as a result of excessive steam pressure."
A6  Gas turbines: "A physical inspection of the bypass system is now planned during the forthcoming
    outage in September 2019 to help determine the root cause of the pressure excursions."
A7  UPS: all UPS units at site functioned correctly to enable continuity of supply to plant equipment;
    the relevant OEMs confirmed this; the operator does not now believe the UPS were related to the
    subsequent trip.
A8  UPS: "RWE's hypothesis is that the UPS' have initiated a changeover to battery back-up supplies as a
    consequence of the system disturbance." The exact characteristic of the power supply to the UPS
    causing it to switch to battery operation is still to be determined and subject to further investigation.
A9  UPS: OEM resilience testing requested during the outage commencing 6 September 2019 [reported],
    cross-referenced to manufacturing tests (9 November 2017) and commissioning tests (January 2018).

DOCUMENT S04 — Little Barford power station shift account, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: RWE Generation, Little Barford station operating staff (roles only; no individuals)
Record type: reconstructed shift narrative and attributed post-event statements (operator, regulator)
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: BST (UTC+01:00). This account adds no clock readings; it gives only the approximate
intervals stated in the published sources, and each interval names the event it is measured from.
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated in published material; [illustrative] texture only,
never a time, MW value or cause (not used in this account); [measured] and [estimated] not used.
Roles: "plant operators" and "operating staff" refer to the station's operational staff on shift.

PART 1 — SHIFT NARRATIVE (reconstructed from published accounts)
Plant state before the disturbance
N1  The station (740 MW [reported] CCGT, connected at Eaton Socon 400 kV [reported] substation) had
    all three units operating: gas turbines GT1A and GT1B and steam turbine ST1C.
Steam turbine trip
N2  At the start of the station's event sequence the 110 V AC UPS -B- and then UPS -A- raised general
    fault alarms (station sequence-of-events record).
N3  Within 1 second [reported] of the lightning strike and the resulting transmission system disturbance,
    steam turbine ST1C tripped while generating 244 MW [reported].
Steam bypass operation
N4  With the steam turbine lost, the plant went into steam bypass mode: steam generated from the gas
    turbines is fed directly into the condenser. This is the normal operation following loss of the
    steam turbine, intended to allow sustained operation of the gas turbines.
N5  Following the steam turbine trip, the pressure in the steam system rose.
First gas turbine trip
N6  Around a minute [reported] after the transmission system fault, gas turbine GT1A (generating
    210 MW [reported]) tripped automatically due to a high-pressure excursion in the steam bypass system.
Second gas turbine trip
N7  The steam system pressure continued to rise after the GT1A trip, and the plant operators made the
    decision to manually trip the other operational gas turbine due to safety risks.
N8  Around 30 seconds [reported] after the GT1A trip, GT1B (187 MW [reported]) was manually tripped by
    the operating staff in response to high steam pressures. Total station loss: 641 MW [reported].

PART 2 — POST-EVENT ANNOTATIONS (attributed, in each source's order; not part of the shift record)
Annotation A — operator report "RWE Preliminary Findings Regarding the Event on 9th August 2019",
dated 30 August 2019:
A1  UPS: "The investigation to date has found that all UPS' at Site have functioned correctly to enable
    continuity of supply to plant equipment." "Therefore, we do not now believe the UPS' were related
    to the subsequent trip."
A2  UPS: "RWE's hypothesis is that the UPS' have initiated a changeover to battery back-up supplies as a
    consequence of the system disturbance. The exact characteristic of the power supply to the UPS
    causing it to switch to battery operation is still to be determined and subject to further
    investigation."
A3  UPS: OEM resilience testing requested during the outage commencing 6 September 2019 [reported].
A4  Steam turbine: "Our investigations have confirmed that the Steam Turbine tripped due to a
    discrepancy in the speed signals after the point of the Transmission System fault clearance."
    A comprehensive investigation of hardware, software, fault handling and diagnostic coverage for
    the conditions the steam turbine was subjected to during this rare system disturbance is ongoing.
A5  Gas turbines: "For reasons presently unknown a high-pressure excursion occurred on GT1A resulting in
    an automated trip. Given the prevailing conditions all systems functioned as expected. GT1B was
    manually tripped shortly after as a result of excessive steam pressure."
A6  Gas turbines: "A physical inspection of the bypass system is now planned during the forthcoming
    outage in September 2019 to help determine the root cause of the pressure excursions."
Annotation B — regulator report, Ofgem "9 August 2019 power outage report", dated 3 January 2020:
B1  3.28: "We have established that the steam turbine tripped initially because of a discrepancy in the
    three [reported] independent speed sensors on the turbine. This discrepancy exceeded the tolerance
    of the control system, causing the generator to automatically shut down. The root cause of the
    discrepancy in the speed sensors has not been established."
B2  3.29: following the steam turbine trip the steam system pressure rose; safety systems automatically
    shut down one of the gas turbines due to excessive pressure in the steam bypass; as the pressure kept
    rising, the plant operators manually tripped the other gas turbine due to safety risks. "The root
    cause of these high pressure conditions has not been established."
B3  3.29: "Given the sequence of events and in absence of an established root cause, it is our
    preliminary view that the steam turbine's anomalous speed readings and the resulting trip were due
    to the transmission network fault following the lightning strike."

DOCUMENT R10 — Operating requirements as described in the published reports (selection)
Owner/originator: compiled from the National Grid ESO, Ofgem and E3C reports; no code administrator text
Record type: reconstruction of requirements as the reports describe them, attributed item by item
STATUS: RECONSTRUCTION OF REQUIREMENTS DESCRIBED IN PUBLISHED REPORTS — NOT CODE OR STANDARD TEXT.
The editions of the Grid Code, SQSS and Distribution Code in force on 9 August 2019 have not been
verified for this exercise. Each item restates what the named report says, not the code's own wording.
Clock reference: no clock times are recorded; dates are calendar dates as printed (UK, BST = UTC+01:00).
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated in the named report; [measured], [estimated],
[modelled], [digitised] and [illustrative] not used.
Sources: ESO technical report dated 6 September 2019 (ESO), its Appendix H (ESO App. H) and answers to
E3C questions (ESO answers; data available on 28 August 2019); Ofgem report dated 3 January 2020
(Ofgem); E3C interim report, October 2019 (E3C interim); E3C final report, January 2020 (E3C final).

SECTION A — SECURITY STANDARD (SQSS): SECURED EVENTS AND FREQUENCY LIMITS
A1   ESO 2.2: the SQSS specifies the limits of frequency deviations for secured events, which include
     loss of output from a single generating unit, CCGT module, boiler, nuclear reactor or DC bi-pole.
     Normal Infeed Loss Risk: maximum frequency deviation should not exceed 0.5 Hz [reported].
     Infrequent Infeed Loss Risk: frequency should not deviate outside the range 49.5 Hz [reported]
     to 50.5 Hz [reported] for more than 60 seconds [reported].
A2   ESO 2.2: the level of the normal infeed loss actually covered depends on the configuration of the
     system at the time (printed as "typically it is c. 1,000W" [reported]); the current normal
     infrequent infeed maximum loss risk is 1,260 MW [reported] for when Sizewell is at full load.
A3   ESO App. H: 'Normal Infeed Loss' is the maximum loss the system should be able to manage without
     the frequency going below 49.5 Hz [reported] (e.g. an interconnector at 1,000 MW [reported]);
     'Infrequent Infeed Loss' is a higher level (e.g. Sizewell at 1,260 MW [reported]) for which the
     frequency should not go below 49.2 Hz [reported] and should recover to 49.5 Hz [reported] within
     one minute.
A4   ESO App. H: the SQSS anticipates only one Secured Event at any one time and does not assume
     multiple Secured Events occurring simultaneously (N-1). The Power Infeed Loss is the power infeed
     that can be lost in one Secured Event: generally a single large generator, or two or more smaller
     generators connected through an asset treated as a single Secured Event (for example a double
     circuit overhead line or busbar).
A5   ESO App. H: the system should be re-secured as soon as reasonably practicable after the occurrence
     of a Secured Event.
A6   ESO glossary: "The current maximum upper limit for an infrequent infeed loss risk is 1800MW." [reported]
A7   Ofgem Box 4: the SQSS requires frequency to stay above or equal to 49.5 Hz [reported], or any fall
     below that level to be recovered within 60 seconds [reported], for such events; the ESO is required
     to secure the system by holding reserves so that the frequency limits are not breached.
A8   E3C final, footnote 14: the SQSS allows a deviation below 49.5 Hz [reported] provided that the
     frequency is returned to 49.5 Hz [reported] within 60 seconds [reported].
A9   Ofgem 3.2 and 3.5: the ESO does not consider it is required to secure against distributed generation
     losses under the SQSS; it follows an internal policy of securing against both transmission-connected
     and vector shift distributed generation losses for credible transmission faults during periods of
     increased risk (e.g. bad weather, lightning) or when it considers it economic to do so.

SECTION B — LARGEST LOSS, RATE OF CHANGE OF FREQUENCY AND VECTOR SHIFT (as ESO describes its practice)
B1   ESO App. H: in securing for the largest loss the ESO takes into account the protection setting
     historically specified in the Distribution Code for RoCoF of 0.125 Hz/s [reported], and seeks to
     ensure the system is configured in real time so that this limit is not breached for an infeed loss.
B2   ESO answer 11: the ESO secures the system to within a RoCoF limit of 0.125 Hz/s [reported] for the
     largest credible loss, and schedules frequency response so that the largest loss is contained to
     49.5 Hz [reported] for a normal loss and 49.2 Hz [reported] for an abnormal loss.
B3   ESO App. H: approximately 2 GW [reported] of small generators are connected to the distribution
     networks via relays which disconnect them if the RoCoF is greater than 0.125 Hz/s [reported].
B4   ESO App. H: approximately 8.5 GW [reported] of small generators are connected via relays which
     disconnect them if the vector shift angle is greater than 6 degrees [reported].
B5   ESO App. H: vector shift risks are divided into Type A (transmission faults with no coincident loss
     of BMU infeed, e.g. an overhead line) and Type B (transmission faults with coincident loss of BMU
     infeed, e.g. a generator busbar). The largest Type A risk is monitored for each half-hourly
     settlement period; Type B faults are only secured where it is economic to do so.

SECTION C — FREQUENCY RESPONSE AND RESERVE PRODUCTS (definitions as ESO describes them)
C1   ESO App. H: primary response must be delivering its required output by 10 seconds [reported]
     following the trip and continue for a further 20 seconds [reported] (30 seconds total).
C2   ESO App. H: secondary response must be delivering its required output by 30 seconds [reported]
     following the change in frequency and continue for a further 30 minutes [reported].
C3   ESO App. H: dynamic response is a continuously provided service to manage normal fluctuations in the
     frequency; static response is provided when the system frequency transgresses the low frequency
     relay setting on site. Both can come from generation and demand, BM and non-BM units.
C4   ESO App. H: Mandatory Frequency Response (MFR) can only be provided by synchronised BM units and is
     an obligation of the Grid Code; commercial response is procured from generation or demand, BM or
     non-BM units, whose providers are required to deliver the contracted amount.
C5   ESO answer 13: Firm Frequency Response (FFR) is tendered for on a monthly basis; Mandatory Frequency
     Response has similar characteristics but is an obligation in a generator's connection agreement;
     Enhanced Frequency Response (EFR) is a faster form of FFR; static frequency response reduces demand
     or increases generation when the frequency hits a trigger limit.
C6   ESO answer 13: reserve services: Short Term Operating Reserve typically delivers energy
     within 20 minutes [reported] or less; Rapid Start provides access to energy in less than
     2 minutes [reported]; Balancing Mechanism actions.
C7   ESO App. H: a minimum amount of dynamic response must be held for steady state frequency control;
     the minimum dynamic response requirement at the time of the incident was set to 550 MW [reported].

SECTION D — LOW FREQUENCY DEMAND DISCONNECTION (LFDD)
D1   ESO 4.3: the Grid Code requires each DNO to make arrangements that will enable automatic
     disconnection of demand if the frequency on the transmission system drops below
     48.8 Hz [reported]; demand is disconnected in staged blocks (5%, 7.5% and 10%) [reported].
D2   E3C final, Table 1 "Low Frequency Demand Disconnection settings for each frequency disconnection
     stages" (% of demand disconnection in each transmission area; an area is listed only where the
     table prints a value): E&W = England & Wales (NGET); SPT = Southern Scotland; SHET = Northern Scotland
     Stage 1 | 48.80 Hz [reported] | E&W 5 [reported]
     Stage 2 | 48.75 Hz [reported] | E&W 5 [reported]
     Stage 3 | 48.70 Hz [reported] | E&W 10 [reported]
     Stage 4 | 48.60 Hz [reported] | E&W 7.5 [reported] | SHET 10 [reported]
     Stage 5 | 48.50 Hz [reported] | E&W 7.5 [reported] | SPT 10 [reported]
     Stage 6 | 48.40 Hz [reported] | E&W 7.5 [reported] | SPT 10 [reported] | SHET 10 [reported]
     Stage 7 | 48.20 Hz [reported] | E&W 7.5 [reported] | SPT 10 [reported] | SHET 10 [reported]
     Stage 8 | 48.00 Hz [reported] | E&W 5 [reported] | SPT 10 [reported] | SHET 10 [reported]
     Stage 9 | 47.80 Hz [reported] | E&W 5 [reported]
     Total % demand | E&W 60 [reported] | SPT 40 [reported] | SHET 40 [reported]
D3   Ofgem 3.38: Grid Code Operating Code 6 requires each DNO in England and Wales to have LFDD equipment
     in place to disconnect a maximum of 60% [reported] of demand (measured at winter demand), operating
     in stages; the requirements contain an accuracy tolerance for the frequency levels and a time delay
     permitted for different LFDD equipment, depending on its installation date.
D4   Ofgem 3.39: Stage 1 of the LFDD required 5% [reported] of winter peak demand to be disconnected.
D5   E3C final, on the 5% [reported] figure: "The 5% demand figure is based on forecasted peak demand
     during an average cold spell."
D6   E3C interim: the scheme is designed to disconnect between 5 - 60% [reported] of total peak demand
     through 9 [reported] stages as the system frequency reaches certain trigger levels.
D7   ESO glossary: LFDD is set up in agreement with the ESO by DNOs to reduce their demand in
     5% [reported] stages of total demand (printed as "up to 40% available") [reported].
D8   Ofgem 3.44: SP Distribution, being part of the SP Transmission network area, is not required by the
     Grid Code to disconnect demand until frequency reaches 48.5 Hz [reported].
D9   ESO 2.5: Grid Code OC6.6 describes the automatic LFDD scheme and the arrangements the DNOs are
     required to make in relation to it; following operation of the scheme, the DNOs must notify ESO of
     its operation and are not permitted to restore automatically disconnected demand without
     instruction from National Grid ESO.
D10  Ofgem 3.40: the Grid Code does not currently regulate the disconnection of distributed generation
     through LFDD.

SECTION E — DISTRIBUTED GENERATION PROTECTION (Distribution Code, as the reports describe it)
E1   E3C final: under the Distribution Code, embedded generators are required to install protection
     which detects when the generator is islanded and safely shuts the plant down, predominantly by
     monitoring the rate of change of frequency or the change in voltage phase angle (vector shift).
E2   E3C final: requirements introduced in 2014 [reported] required all generators with a capacity
     greater than 5 MW [reported] to install RoCoF protection with specific settings; this was
     implemented across all relevant sites in 2018 [reported], and the Accelerated Loss of Mains
     Protection programme was initiated in 2019 [reported] for embedded generators between
     5 MW and 50 kW [reported].
E3   Ofgem, footnote 18: vector shift protection is no longer permitted for distributed generators
     connected after 1 February 2018 [reported].
E4   Ofgem 3.32: Distribution Code changes reduced the frequency level triggering under frequency
     protections to 47 Hz [reported], permitted for distributed generators with capacities greater
     than 5 MW [reported] from August 2010 [reported].

DOCUMENT S07 — ESO control room log, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: National Grid ESO, Electricity National Control Centre (ENCC); roles only, no individuals
Record type: reconstructed control-room timeline, per-area communication times and attributed annotations
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: times as printed by ESO, which labels no clock; read as BST (UTC+01:00) because ESO
dates the event at 4:52pm. Entries keep the precision the source prints (seconds, minutes or "Approx").
Value-status legend: [reported] value or time as stated in ESO's published material; [measured],
[estimated], [modelled], [digitised] and [illustrative] not used.
Balancing Mechanism acceptances issued by the room are not transcribed in this record; the published
acceptance data (Elexon BOALF, evidence R06) and the calls drawn on ESO's Appendix J call diagram
(evidence R08) are listed as separate entries of this room's control log.

PART 1 — TIMELINE ENTRIES COMPILED BY ESO AFTER THE EVENT (technical report dated 6 September 2019,
Table 1; operational rows whose source column reads ESO, and the closing row sourced to the DNOs)
E01  16:52:26 [reported]  Frequency at 50.0 Hz [reported]; ESO securing for a loss of power infeed of
     1000 MW [reported].
E02  16:52:34 [reported]  Frequency response initiates.
E03  16:52:44 [reported]  Frequency response has delivered at least 650 MW [reported] of power to
     stabilise the frequency.
E04  16:52:58 [reported]  Frequency drop is arrested at 49.1 Hz [reported] due to the delivery of
     frequency response products.
E05  16:52 [reported]  Contracted response service from Low Frequency Gas Turbines initiated.
E06  16:53:04 [reported]  Frequency response has delivered 900 MW [reported] of power to stabilise the
     frequency.
E07  Since 16:53 [reported]  Short Term Operating Reserve (STOR) units were instructed; overall amount
     400 MW [reported].
E08  16:53:18 [reported]  Frequency recovers to 49.2 Hz [reported], due to the continued delivery of
     frequency response.
E09  16:53:31 [reported]  All frequency response is being delivered at this point attempting to restore
     the frequency to operational limits.
E10  16:54:20 [reported]  Control room initiate instructions to generation to restore the system
     frequency and response levels to stabilise the system.
E11  16:57:15 [reported]  Frequency returns to 50 Hz [reported] following over 1,000 MW [reported] of
     response and a further 1240 MW [reported] of control room actions to restore frequency and
     stabilise the situation.
E12  16:58 – 17:16 [reported]  ESO progressively instructs the DNOs that they can commence demand
     restoration.

findings.statement: Three lightning strikes were recorded at 2019-08-09T16:52:33.490+01:00 (UTC+01:00, BST) adjacent to the Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main 400 kV transmission circuit near Willian Arboretum, Letchworth Garden City.

The largest of the three simultaneous lightning strikes had a current amplitude of 33.7 kA and one of the three strikes is confirmed as the cause of the 400 kV circuit fault by NGET analysis overlaying MeteoGroup lightning location data with the fault location.

The fault was a single-phase to earth fault on the blue phase, located approximately 4.5 km from Wymondley Main substation, with an estimated 50% voltage depression at the fault location lasting approximately 100 ms.
The fault infeed was approximately 21 kA (RMS) from Wymondley Main and approximately 7 kA (RMS) from Eaton Socon.
The Wymondley Main end of the Eaton Socon–Wymondley circuit breaker opened at 2019-08-09T16:52:33.560+01:00, clearing the fault in 70 ms after fault inception.

The Eaton Socon end of the circuit breaker opened at 2019-08-09T16:52:33.564+01:00, clearing the fault in 74 ms after fault inception, both within the 80 ms Grid Code requirement for 400 kV primary protection.

Following the event, engineers attended Wymondley Main and Eaton Socon substations and found all assets operating as normal with no defects identified; a visual inspection of the overhead line on 10 August 2019 revealed no defects.
The Eaton Socon–Wymondley circuit was automatically re-energized on Delayed Auto-Reclose (DAR) at 2019-08-09T16:52:53+01:00, returning it to service approximately 20 seconds after the fault.

After the DAR reclose, the network was in the same configuration as before the event; no further operational intervention or immediate site attendance was required, and the circuit performed normally.

Before the event, Hornsea One was generating 799 MW, comprised of modules 1B and 1C each at 400 MW operating at their maximum, and module 1A at an estimated 62 MW, with one Static Generator Transformer (SGT) and one offshore transmission system user asset (OTSUA) circuit on outage.

Beginning at 15:52:33.490Z (2019-08-09T16:52:33.490+01:00), Hornsea One's reactive power compensation initially injected leading MVAr to boost NETS voltage, then oscillated dramatically, at one point absorbing more than 300 MVAr while the NETS and Hornsea One system voltage fell to approximately 394 kV.
In the Hornsea 1B 34 kV collection cable system, the voltage rapidly reduced to approximately 20 kV (target 34 kV) during the disturbance.

findings.derivation: 799 MW initial output minus 62 MW final output = 737 MW loss

quantity.basis: reported: 799 MW before minus 62 MW after

findings.statement: Hornsea One 1B and 1C wind turbine generators began de-loading at 15:52:33.728Z (2019-08-09T16:52:33.728+01:00) and completed de-load of all turbines on those modules to 0 MW within 107 ms, while 1A remained in operation at 62 MW, resulting in a loss of 737 MW from pre-event 799 MW.

Hornsea One's turbine de-loading resulted from wind turbine controllers reacting to the voltage fluctuations on the offshore network by automatically shutting down, rather than performing the fault ride-through they were designed for.

Hornsea One's de-load was caused by an insufficiently damped electrical resonance in the sub-synchronous frequency range, which was triggered by the initial fault, with similar damped oscillations having occurred approximately 10 minutes before the event without causing de-loading at that time.

The Hornsea One offshore control system operated as designed; the root cause of the control system's destabilizing response lies in the wind turbine controller settings which were standard settings from the manufacturer.

Before the event, Little Barford power station was generating 641 MW total, composed of steam turbine ST1C generating 244 MW, gas turbine GT1A generating 210 MW, and gas turbine GT1B generating 187 MW.

Little Barford's steam turbine ST1C began shutdown at the station's sequence-of-events datum T, approximately 2019-08-09T16:52:34+01:00 ±0.5 s, triggered by a discrepancy in the three independent speed sensors that exceeded the control system's tolerance; the generator breaker opened at T+1.185 s.

The root cause of the discrepancy in the three independent speed sensors on Little Barford's steam turbine has not been established, although both RWE and Ofgem attribute the anomalous readings to the transmission system disturbance.

Little Barford gas turbine GT1A automatically tripped approximately 56.6 seconds after the sequence-of-events datum T (approximately 2019-08-09T16:53:30+01:00) due to a high-pressure excursion in the steam bypass system; the exact cause of this high pressure is unknown despite all systems functioning as expected.

Little Barford gas turbine GT1B was manually tripped by station operators approximately 83.9 seconds after the sequence-of-events datum T (approximately 2019-08-09T16:53:58+01:00), approximately 30 seconds after GT1A, due to continued high pressure in the steam bypass system presenting safety risks; the root cause of the pressure conditions has not been established.
The system frequency reached a minimum of 48.787 Hz at 2019-08-09T16:53:49+01:00, representing a total frequency drop of 1.213 Hz from 50.0 Hz over approximately 76 seconds from the lightning strike.
The largest single-second frequency drops occurred immediately after fault inception, with a drop of 0.151 Hz between 2019-08-09T16:52:35+01:00 (49.770 Hz) and 2019-08-09T16:52:36+01:00 (49.633 Hz).
At 2019-08-09T16:52:44+01:00, the frequency response products had delivered at least 650 MW of power, arresting the frequency drop at approximately 49.1 Hz by 2019-08-09T16:52:58+01:00.
By 2019-08-09T16:53:04+01:00, the ESO's frequency response products had delivered 900 MW of power to continue stabilizing the frequency.

The system frequency excursion complied with SQSS infrequent infeed loss risk limits (frequency should not go below 49.2 Hz and should recover to 49.5 Hz within 60 seconds), though it exceeded the normal infeed loss risk limit (should remain above or equal to 49.5 Hz).

findings.statement: Ofgem's final report (3 January 2020) reported 892 MW of net demand was disconnected from local distribution networks as a result of LFDD, representing approximately 4% of national demand and affecting 1.15 million customers.
The LFDD disconnection affected approximately 1.15 million customers across all distribution network operator areas.
By DNO area, the demand disconnected by LFDD ranged from 0 MW in SHEPD to 190 MW in WPD West Midlands, with intermediate values varying by area and network configuration.
The first report of demand disconnection from a distribution network operator was received by the ESO control room at 2019-08-09T16:56+01:00, approximately 4 minutes after the lightning strike.

The ESO progressively instructed DNOs to commence demand restoration beginning at 2019-08-09T16:58+01:00 and continuing to 2019-08-09T17:16+01:00, requiring restoration in a staged progressive manner rather than automatic reconnection.
The earliest reports of demand restoration at individual locations came from WPD South West and UKPN London, reported at 2019-08-09T16:56+01:00 and 2019-08-09T16:58+01:00 respectively.
The first DNO reported that its demand had been fully restored at 2019-08-09T17:07+01:00, approximately 15 minutes after the initial fault.
Individual DNO areas completed demand restoration at different times, ranging from 2019-08-09T17:07+01:00 (earliest by various DNOs) to 2019-08-09T17:37+01:00 (latest, UKPN and WPD areas).
All distribution network operators had confirmed that demand restoration had been completed by 2019-08-09T17:37+01:00, approximately 45 minutes after the initial lightning strike and fault.
The ESO control room established communication with distribution network operators and the NGET control room within 2 minutes of the initial transmission system fault.

Operational communications during the demand restoration process were generally efficient and effective, and the ESO control room experienced no communication system failures; verbal instructions to DNOs to restore demand, though not following agreed phraseology, were clear and understood.

report.executive_summary: On 9 August 2019 at 16:52:33 BST (UTC+01:00), a lightning strike adjacent to the 400 kV Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main transmission circuit caused a single-phase fault to earth, triggering automatic protection. The circuit breakers operated within 74 ms (within the 80 ms Grid Code requirement) and the circuit was restored by delayed auto-reclose after 20 seconds. The disturbance caused two distinct but interrelated generation losses totalling approximately 1,378 MW: Hornsea One wind farm lost 737 MW through automatic turbine de-loading within 107 ms due to control system instability triggered by voltage oscillations; Little Barford power station lost 641 MW through sequential tripping of its steam and gas turbines. The system frequency fell from 50 Hz to a minimum of 48.787 Hz within 76 seconds, spending 32 seconds below 49 Hz. This frequency excursion triggered low-frequency demand disconnection (LFDD) relays across distribution networks, disconnecting 892–973 MW of demand from 1.15 million customers. Frequency response and reserve services delivered over 1,000 MW of generation support and restored frequency to 50 Hz within 285 seconds. Demand restoration proceeded gradually over 40 minutes, with the first circuits restored at 17:07 BST and final restoration at 17:37 BST. The transmission protection, frequency response services, LFDD scheme and demand restoration all performed according to their design requirements, though several underlying causes of generation loss remain incompletely explained.

sections.body:
The event began with three simultaneous lightning strikes recorded at 2019-08-09T16:52:33.490+01:00 (BST) adjacent to the Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main 400 kV transmission circuit near Willian Arboretum, with the largest strike having a current amplitude of 33.7 kA [F01, F02]. One of these strikes caused a single-phase to earth fault on the blue phase of the circuit approximately 4.5 km from Wymondley Main substation, with an estimated 50% voltage depression at the fault location [F03].

The fault current was approximately 21 kA from Wymondley Main and 7 kA from Eaton Socon [F04]. The transmission protection system responded automatically: the Wymondley Main end opened in 70 ms and the Eaton Socon end in 74 ms after fault inception, both within the 80 ms Grid Code requirement [F05, F06]. There were no defects identified in the protection system or at the substations following the event [F07]. The circuit was automatically re-energized by the delayed auto-reclose system approximately 20 seconds after the fault [F08], returning the network to its pre-fault configuration [F09]. The protection operated as designed and the circuit afterfault performed normally.
sections.heading: Initiating Event: Transmission Fault and Circuit Clearance

sections.body:
Before the fault, Hornsea One was generating 799 MW (1B and 1C modules at 400 MW each, 1A at an estimated ~62 MW, with one SGT and one OTSUA on outage creating a weak internal network) [F10]. The voltage disturbance triggered wind turbine control system instability beginning at 15:52:33.490Z (UTC): reactive power compensation injected leading MVAr initially, then oscillated dramatically, absorbing >300 MVAr at one point while the system voltage fell to approximately 394 kV [F11]. The 34 kV offshore collection voltage fell to approximately 20 kV [F12]. 

Wind turbine de-loading began 238 ms after the voltage dip (15:52:33.728Z) and completed 107 ms later (15:52:33.835Z), with 1B and 1C modules (797 MW total) reduced to zero output while 1A remained at 62 MW [F13]. This loss of 737 MW resulted from wind turbine controllers reacting to voltage fluctuations with inappropriate protection actions rather than fault ride-through [F14]. The operator's investigation concluded this was caused by insufficiently damped sub-synchronous oscillations in the electrical resonance triggered by the fault, which had not previously caused de-loading despite similar oscillations being observed approximately 10 minutes beforehand [F15]. The offshore control system had operated as designed; the root cause of the control system's response lies in turbine controller settings [F16].
sections.heading: Generation Loss: Hornsea One Offshore Wind Farm

sections.body:
Little Barford was generating 641 MW before the event (ST1C 244 MW, GT1A 210 MW, GT1B 187 MW) [F17]. The first loss occurred at the station's sequence-of-events datum T ≈ 2019-08-09T16:52:34+01:00 (±0.5 s), when the steam turbine control system detected speed signal anomalies and initiated shutdown; the ST1C breaker opened at T+1.185 s with 244 MW loss [F18]. 

This was caused by a discrepancy in the three independent speed sensors exceeding the controller's tolerance, which the operator and Ofgem attribute to the transmission system disturbance but whose root cause has not been established [F19]. Following ST1C loss, steam generated by the gas turbines backed up into the condensers in bypass mode. Gas turbine GT1A automatically tripped at approximately T+56.6 s (around one minute after the fault) due to high-pressure excursion in the steam system; the exact trigger is unknown despite all systems functioning as expected [F20]. Following continued pressure rise, the plant operators manually tripped GT1B at T+83.9 s (~30 seconds after GT1A) due to safety risks from excessive steam pressure [F21]. This resulted in a total station loss of 641 MW within approximately 84 seconds of the fault.
sections.heading: Generation Loss: Little Barford Power Station

sections.body:
The system frequency fell from 50.0 Hz at 16:52:26 BST (when the ESO was securing for a 1,000 MW loss) to a minimum of 48.787 Hz at 2019-08-09T16:53:49+01:00 [F22], representing a 1.213 Hz drop over 83 seconds. The largest single-second drops occurred immediately after fault inception (0.151 Hz drop from 49.921 to 49.770 Hz at 16:52:35) [F23].

The frequency decline was arrested at 49.1 Hz by 16:52:58 when frequency response products delivered at least 650 MW [F24]. By 16:53:04 this had increased to 900 MW of delivered response [F25]. The system remained below 49.5 Hz SQSS limit for the normal infeed loss risk but complied with the infrequent infeed loss risk limits (49.2 Hz minimum, 60-second recovery) [F26]. Frequency was below 49.0 Hz for 32 seconds (16:53:41 to 16:54:13+01:00) and recovered to 50.0 Hz at 2019-08-09T16:57:15+01:00 [F27], some 162 seconds after reaching minimum and 282 seconds after the initial fault.

The ESO held system inertia of approximately 219.6 GVA.s immediately prior to the trip (estimated, reported), with the holding of 1,022 MW of frequency response products before the event [F28]. Following the loss of the two largest generation units, the system delivered over 1,000 MW of frequency response plus a further 1,240 MW through ESO control room actions including Short Term Operating Reserve, Rapid Start, Balancing Mechanism actions and Fast Reserve [F29].
sections.heading: Frequency Excursion and Containment

sections.body:
When system frequency fell below 48.8 Hz (the Stage 1 LFDD trigger threshold), automatic demand disconnection relays operated across distribution networks, based on Grid Code requirements for DNOs to arrange automatic disconnection in staged blocks [F30]. The actual minimum frequency was 48.787 Hz, just below this trigger.

The reported demand disconnected figures vary by source: the ESO technical report cites 931 MW disconnected [F31]; the E3C interim report cites 973 MW [F32]; and the Ofgem final report cites 892 MW net demand [F33]. These variations reflect different accounting bases and timing of reports (ESO data as of 13 August 2019 at 12:00; E3C and Ofgem including various adjustments). The disconnection affected approximately 1.15 million customers across all DNO areas [F34]. By DNO area, the disconnection ranged from 0 MW (SHEPD) to 190 MW (WPD West Midlands) [F35]. The first report of demand disconnection reached the ESO control room at 16:56+01:00 [F36].

sections.body: The ESO progressively instructed demand restoration beginning at 16:58+01:00 and continuing to 17:16+01:00, requiring DNOs to restore in a staged manner and not automatically [F37]. Restoration began at different times by DNO: WPD South West and UKPN London reported earliest restoration at 16:56–16:58+01:00 [F38]. The first DNO reported completion at 17:07+01:00 [F39], with individual DNO areas completing between 17:07 and 17:37+01:00 [F40]. All demand restoration had been confirmed complete by 17:37+01:00, approximately 45 minutes after the initial fault [F41]. This restoration proceeded whilst frequency was still being stabilized and represents demand being reconnected as system conditions allowed, distinct from the recovery of other affected generation services.

sections.body:
**Little Barford steam turbine speed signal discrepancy:** The root cause of the three independent speed sensors showing readings that exceeded the control system's tolerance has not been established. RWE and Ofgem attribute this to the transmission disturbance but the mechanism remains unknown [F19].

**Little Barford gas turbine high-pressure excursions:** The mechanism causing the high-pressure buildup in the steam bypass system that led to the automatic trip of GT1A and manual trip of GT1B is unresolved. RWE planned physical inspection of the bypass system in September 2019 to investigate [F20, F21].

**Hornsea One wind turbine control instability:** While the operator identified insufficiently damped sub-synchronous oscillations as the trigger, the root cause of why the wind turbine controller settings allowed this specific oscillatory response is not definitively established, particularly given that similar oscillations had been observed 10 minutes earlier without causing de-loading [F15, F16].

**Demand disconnection accounting differences:** The variation in reported demand disconnected (892–973 MW) reflects different accounting bases, data collection times, and definitions used by ESO, E3C and Ofgem. The actual instantaneous demand disconnected cannot be precisely determined from the evidence [F33].

**LFDD trigger timing precision:** The exact time at which frequency crossed the 48.8 Hz LFDD threshold cannot be determined from the 1-second frequency samples, though the minimum of 48.787 Hz was reached at 16:53:49+01:00 [F22].
sections.heading: Unexplained Causes and Uncertainties

sections.body:
**Transmission fault causation:** The lightning strike is confirmed as the cause by NGET analysis overlaying MeteoGroup strike location data with the fault location and timing, and is supported by the time alignment of one recorded strike with the fault inception [F01, F02].

**Transmission protection:** The protection system operated within all Grid Code requirements, with both ends clearing the fault in under 75 ms against an 80 ms requirement [F05, F06]. The circuit performed normally after re-energization [F09].

**Frequency response:** The frequency response products held and delivered by the system (650 MW by 16:52:44, 900 MW by 16:53:04, over 1,000 MW total) stabilized the frequency decline and held it to the required limits under the infrequent infeed loss risk standard [F26, F29].

**LFDD performance:** The demand disconnection occurred at the correct trigger threshold (48.8 Hz) and in the correct sequence of stages [F30]. This is supported by the Grid Code requirements and by all DNO reports [F31, F32, F33].

**Demand restoration coordination:** The ESO control room established communications with DNOs within 2 minutes of the fault and issued progressive restoration instructions that were clearly understood and efficiently executed, with no communication system failures [F42, F43].
sections.heading: Supported Explanations and Requirements Compliance

sections.body:
**Clock alignment discrepancies:** Little Barford's sequence-of-events datum T (approximately 16:52:34+01:00 ±0.5 s) has not been aligned with the ESO system operator's clock; events at Little Barford carry timing uncertainty of approximately 1 second [F18].

**Hornsea One event timing:** Some event times in the operator's published timeline were given only to the minute; specific times were inferred from operator annotations and are marked as estimated [F12, F13].

**Demand disconnection magnitude:** Three different official figures exist (931 MW, 973 MW, 892 MW) reflecting different accounting bases, collection times, and definitions by different organizations [F33]. The true instantaneous demand disconnected cannot be determined precisely.

**Chart-derived values:** Hornsea One voltage and power values are digitized from published chart images and carry stated digitization uncertainties; these are not original measurement records [F11, F12].

**Frequency minimum precision:** The measured frequency record has 1-second resolution; the actual frequency minimum between samples cannot be determined [F22].

**System inertia estimate:** The inertia value immediately prior to the trip (219.6 GVA.s) is estimated using a model, not directly measured; ESO does not currently measure inertia directly [F28].

The ESO technical report (6 September 2019) reported that 931 MW of demand was automatically disconnected by LFDD relay operation, based on DNO reported data as of 13 August 2019 at 12:00, representing 3.2% of the national transmission demand of 29 GW at the time.

quantity.basis: reported by E3C interim report Table 1

findings.statement: The Energy Emergencies Executive Committee (E3C) interim report reported 973 MW of demand disconnected by LFDD as reported by DNO areas.

quantity.basis: reported by Ofgem as net demand

findings.statement: Ofgem's final report (3 January 2020) reported 892 MW of net demand was disconnected from local distribution networks as a result of LFDD, representing approximately 4% of national demand and affecting 1.15 million customers.
The LFDD disconnection affected approximately 1.15 million customers across all distribution network operator areas.
By DNO area, the demand disconnected by LFDD ranged from 0 MW in SHEPD to 190 MW in WPD West Midlands, with intermediate values varying by area and network configuration.

The first report of demand disconnection from a distribution network operator was received by the ESO control room at 2019-08-09T16:56:00.000+01:00, approximately 4 minutes after the lightning strike.

The ESO progressively instructed DNOs to commence demand restoration beginning at 2019-08-09T16:58:00.000+01:00 and continuing to 2019-08-09T17:16:00.000+01:00, requiring restoration in a staged progressive manner rather than automatic reconnection.
The earliest reports of demand restoration at individual locations came from WPD South West at 2019-08-09T16:56:00.000+01:00 and UKPN London at 2019-08-09T16:58:00.000+01:00 respectively.
The first DNO reported that its demand had been fully restored at 2019-08-09T17:07:00.000+01:00, approximately 15 minutes after the initial fault.

Individual DNO areas completed demand restoration at different times, ranging from 2019-08-09T17:07:00.000+01:00 (earliest by various DNOs) to 2019-08-09T17:37:00.000+01:00 (latest, UKPN and WPD areas).
All distribution network operators had confirmed that demand restoration had been completed by 2019-08-09T17:37:00.000+01:00, approximately 45 minutes after the initial lightning strike and fault.
The ESO control room established communication with distribution network operators and the NGET control room within 2 minutes of the initial transmission system fault.

Operational communications during the demand restoration process were generally efficient and effective, and the ESO control room experienced no communication system failures; verbal instructions to DNOs to restore demand, though not following agreed phraseology, were clear and understood.

report.executive_summary: On 9 August 2019 at 16:52:33 BST (UTC+01:00), a lightning strike adjacent to the 400 kV Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main transmission circuit caused a single-phase fault to earth, triggering automatic protection. The circuit breakers operated within 74 ms (within the 80 ms Grid Code requirement) and the circuit was restored by delayed auto-reclose after 20 seconds. The disturbance caused two distinct but interrelated generation losses totalling approximately 1,378 MW: Hornsea One wind farm lost 737 MW through automatic turbine de-loading within 107 ms due to control system instability triggered by voltage oscillations; Little Barford power station lost 641 MW through sequential tripping of its steam and gas turbines. The system frequency fell from 50 Hz to a minimum of 48.787 Hz within 76 seconds, spending 32 seconds below 49 Hz. This frequency excursion triggered low-frequency demand disconnection (LFDD) relays across distribution networks, disconnecting 892–973 MW of demand from 1.15 million customers. Frequency response and reserve services delivered over 1,000 MW of generation support and restored frequency to 50 Hz within 285 seconds. Demand restoration proceeded gradually over 40 minutes, with the first circuits restored at 17:07 BST and final restoration at 17:37 BST. The transmission protection, frequency response services, LFDD scheme and demand restoration all performed according to their design requirements, though several underlying causes of generation loss remain incompletely explained.

sections.body:
The event began with three simultaneous lightning strikes recorded at 2019-08-09T16:52:33.490+01:00 (BST) adjacent to the Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main 400 kV transmission circuit near Willian Arboretum, with the largest strike having a current amplitude of 33.7 kA [F01, F02]. One of these strikes caused a single-phase to earth fault on the blue phase of the circuit approximately 4.5 km from Wymondley Main substation, with an estimated 50% voltage depression at the fault location [F03].

The fault current was approximately 21 kA from Wymondley Main and 7 kA from Eaton Socon [F04]. The transmission protection system responded automatically: the Wymondley Main end opened in 70 ms and the Eaton Socon end in 74 ms after fault inception, both within the 80 ms Grid Code requirement [F05, F06]. There were no defects identified in the protection system or at the substations following the event [F07]. The circuit was automatically re-energized by the delayed auto-reclose system approximately 20 seconds after the fault [F08], returning the network to its pre-fault configuration [F09]. The protection operated as designed and the circuit afterfault performed normally.
sections.heading: Initiating Event: Transmission Fault and Circuit Clearance

sections.body:
Before the fault, Hornsea One was generating 799 MW (1B and 1C modules at 400 MW each, 1A at an estimated ~62 MW, with one SGT and one OTSUA on outage creating a weak internal network) [F10]. The voltage disturbance triggered wind turbine control system instability beginning at 15:52:33.490Z (UTC): reactive power compensation injected leading MVAr initially, then oscillated dramatically, absorbing >300 MVAr at one point while the system voltage fell to approximately 394 kV [F11]. The 34 kV offshore collection voltage fell to approximately 20 kV [F12]. 

Wind turbine de-loading began 238 ms after the voltage dip (15:52:33.728Z) and completed 107 ms later (15:52:33.835Z), with 1B and 1C modules (797 MW total) reduced to zero output while 1A remained at 62 MW [F13]. This loss of 737 MW resulted from wind turbine controllers reacting to voltage fluctuations with inappropriate protection actions rather than fault ride-through [F14]. The operator's investigation concluded this was caused by insufficiently damped sub-synchronous oscillations in the electrical resonance triggered by the fault, which had not previously caused de-loading despite similar oscillations being observed approximately 10 minutes beforehand [F15]. The offshore control system had operated as designed; the root cause of the control system's response lies in turbine controller settings [F16].
sections.heading: Generation Loss: Hornsea One Offshore Wind Farm

sections.body:
Little Barford was generating 641 MW before the event (ST1C 244 MW, GT1A 210 MW, GT1B 187 MW) [F17]. The first loss occurred at the station's sequence-of-events datum T ≈ 2019-08-09T16:52:34+01:00 (±0.5 s), when the steam turbine control system detected speed signal anomalies and initiated shutdown; the ST1C breaker opened at T+1.185 s with 244 MW loss [F18]. 

This was caused by a discrepancy in the three independent speed sensors exceeding the controller's tolerance, which the operator and Ofgem attribute to the transmission system disturbance but whose root cause has not been established [F19]. Following ST1C loss, steam generated by the gas turbines backed up into the condensers in bypass mode. Gas turbine GT1A automatically tripped at approximately T+56.6 s (around one minute after the fault) due to high-pressure excursion in the steam system; the exact trigger is unknown despite all systems functioning as expected [F20]. Following continued pressure rise, the plant operators manually tripped GT1B at T+83.9 s (~30 seconds after GT1A) due to safety risks from excessive steam pressure [F21]. This resulted in a total station loss of 641 MW within approximately 84 seconds of the fault.
sections.heading: Generation Loss: Little Barford Power Station

sections.body:
The system frequency fell from 50.0 Hz at 16:52:26 BST (when the ESO was securing for a 1,000 MW loss) to a minimum of 48.787 Hz at 2019-08-09T16:53:49+01:00 [F22], representing a 1.213 Hz drop over 83 seconds. The largest single-second drops occurred immediately after fault inception (0.151 Hz drop from 49.921 to 49.770 Hz at 16:52:35) [F23].

The frequency decline was arrested at 49.1 Hz by 16:52:58 when frequency response products delivered at least 650 MW [F24]. By 16:53:04 this had increased to 900 MW of delivered response [F25]. The system remained below 49.5 Hz SQSS limit for the normal infeed loss risk but complied with the infrequent infeed loss risk limits (49.2 Hz minimum, 60-second recovery) [F26]. Frequency was below 49.0 Hz for 32 seconds (16:53:41 to 16:54:13+01:00) and recovered to 50.0 Hz at 2019-08-09T16:57:15+01:00 [F27], some 162 seconds after reaching minimum and 282 seconds after the initial fault.

The ESO held system inertia of approximately 219.6 GVA.s immediately prior to the trip (estimated, reported), with the holding of 1,022 MW of frequency response products before the event [F28]. Following the loss of the two largest generation units, the system delivered over 1,000 MW of frequency response plus a further 1,240 MW through ESO control room actions including Short Term Operating Reserve, Rapid Start, Balancing Mechanism actions and Fast Reserve [F29].
sections.heading: Frequency Excursion and Containment

sections.body:
When system frequency fell below 48.8 Hz (the Stage 1 LFDD trigger threshold), automatic demand disconnection relays operated across distribution networks, based on Grid Code requirements for DNOs to arrange automatic disconnection in staged blocks [F30]. The actual minimum frequency was 48.787 Hz, just below this trigger.

The reported demand disconnected figures vary by source: the ESO technical report cites 931 MW disconnected [F31]; the E3C interim report cites 973 MW [F32]; and the Ofgem final report cites 892 MW net demand [F33]. These variations reflect different accounting bases and timing of reports (ESO data as of 13 August 2019 at 12:00; E3C and Ofgem including various adjustments). The disconnection affected approximately 1.15 million customers across all DNO areas [F34]. By DNO area, the disconnection ranged from 0 MW (SHEPD) to 190 MW (WPD West Midlands) [F35]. The first report of demand disconnection reached the ESO control room at 16:56:00+01:00 [F36].
sections.heading: Low Frequency Demand Disconnection

sections.body: The ESO progressively instructed demand restoration beginning at 16:58:00+01:00 and continuing to 17:16:00+01:00, requiring DNOs to restore in a staged manner and not automatically [F37]. Restoration began at different times by DNO: WPD South West and UKPN London reported earliest restoration at 16:56:00+01:00 to 16:58:00+01:00 [F38]. The first DNO reported completion at 17:07:00+01:00 [F39], with individual DNO areas completing between 17:07:00 and 17:37:00+01:00 [F40]. All demand restoration had been confirmed complete by 17:37:00+01:00, approximately 45 minutes after the initial fault [F41]. This restoration proceeded whilst frequency was still being stabilized and represents demand being reconnected as system conditions allowed, distinct from the recovery of other affected generation services.
sections.heading: Demand Restoration
